meta.title: ProjectStore — code changes, context stays
hero.p.1: Decisions, specs, epics and stories live as Markdown in git. ProjectStore takes your agent in Claude Code or Codex from a task to checked code, through the process engineering teams have used for decades. Now it takes minutes.

bar.span.1: Not chat memory. A way of working.
principle.h2.1:
Do not explain it again.
Continue from where it stopped.
principle.p.1: A chat remembers what you talked about. ProjectStore records what the team decided, why, and how to check the result. The next agent, the next model or you in six months read dated decisions and the options you turned down. Not a chat log.
principle.span.3: The decision and its alternatives in an ADR.
principle.span.5: A spec, an epic and a story with clear criteria.
why.h2.1:
The industry invented this long ago.
Agents made it cheap.
why.p.1: ADRs, reviews, a backlog, acceptance criteria, links from goal to code. Mature engineering teams have worked this way for twenty years. ProjectStore invents none of it.
why.p.2: Look at any mature engineering team. Before anything is built, someone writes the decision down and others discuss it. The work is split into stories in a backlog. Each story has acceptance criteria. Each requirement can be traced to the code. The backlog comes from Scrum in 1995. Stories and acceptance tests come from XP in 1999. ADRs, short records of a decision and its reasons, come from Michael Nygard in 2011. Design reviews and RFCs are older still.
why.p.3: The process works. Its documents are the most valuable thing a company keeps after a project: why the system is built this way, what counted as done, where each feature lives in the code. But when people run it by hand, it is slow. An ADR takes an afternoon to write and a week to get reviewed. Documents fall behind the code. The board stops matching reality. So teams cut corners, and "agile" becomes an excuse to write nothing down.
why.p.4: The process was always valuable. What was expensive was people running every step of it.
why.p.5: Agents are the opposite. Writing an ADR, splitting an epic into stories or checking a diff against criteria takes an agent minutes, not days. What an agent lacks is what people get for free: memory between sessions, context shared with colleagues, the link from a goal to the code. Every new session starts empty and decides again what was already settled.
why.p.6: ProjectStore puts the two together. Agent speed makes the old process cheap for the first time. Its documents, kept in files beside the code, give agents what they never had: the project's context, linked up to the goals and down to the code. Every step is checked by a second agent that did not write the draft. Speed gets a memory, and memory gets a check.

why.div.6: ADR, Michael Nygard, 2011. Before that, architecture boards and design review.
why.div.7: An afternoon to write, a week in the review queue. The rejected alternatives stay in someone's head.
why.div.8: The agent drafts it in a minute. A separate critic looks for weak spots. You approve. The result is a dated file that also records what was rejected.
why.div.10: Spec, design doc, RFC. RFCs have been numbered since 1969; design docs are the norm in large companies.
why.div.11: Takes a week to write and is stale by release. Nobody checks that the code still matches it.
why.div.12: A spec lists the expected behaviour as numbered rules. Its checks apply to every story it covers. A story cannot close while its spec is still a draft.
why.div.14: Product backlog from Scrum, 1995. User stories from XP, 1999. Kanban for software, 2007.
why.div.15: Grooming meetings. The board drifts from reality within a week because it is maintained by hand.
why.div.16: Each story file holds its own status. The board, indexes and link map are built from those files. If they drift, one command rebuilds them.
why.div.18: Technical design, impact analysis. The tech lead looks at where this lands in the existing code.
why.div.19: Knowledge of how earlier features landed in the code exists only in the tech lead's head. They are on holiday.
why.div.20: The planner looks at where earlier epics landed in the code. It says where the change belongs and what to reuse. The plan goes into the story.
why.div.22: Acceptance criteria, Definition of Done. XP and Scrum, early 2000s.
why.div.23: A QA cycle at the end of the sprint. "Done" by declaration; criteria spot-checked.
why.div.24: The reviewer checks the diff against every criterion and asks for proof: a test, a command that was run, a line of code. No proof, no close.
why.div.26: Requirements traceability. Mandatory in avionics since DO-178B (1992) and in medical software.
why.div.27: An Excel matrix "requirement → code → test" that nobody updates after the second release.
why.div.28: Every story links up to its epic, ADRs and specs, and down to its code. Proof sits under each acceptance criterion. The link map and the code map are generated, so nobody maintains them by hand.
why.h3.1: The links an agent gets for free: from goal to proof

why.p.7: The links live in the header of each file, and the proof is a line under each acceptance criterion. The agent fills all of it in as it works. The link map shows what each document connects to. The code map shows where each epic's code lives. A new session, a new model or a new colleague starts from this chain, not from nothing.
workflow.p.1: Not one long "do everything" session. Six steps, each with a result and a check. Click a node in the diagram or a tab.
workflow.span.2: The loop: gather context → act → verify · over the project, not just the code
workflow.title.1: The ProjectStore loop: task, document, critic, your approval, backlog, story, planner, code, reviewer, done. Then the board and maps update, and the next session starts with full context.
workflow.text.6: board and maps rebuild → the next session starts where this one ended
workflow.figcaption.1: Lime nodes are checks by an agent that did not write the draft. The diamond is your Yes: nothing is saved before it.
workflow.h3.1: Before code, write the task down.
workflow.p.2: The agent finds where the task fits in the project. A decision becomes an ADR: a short record of what was chosen and why. Expected behaviour becomes a spec, the rules the code must follow. The work becomes an epic and a story with acceptance criteria. Nothing is saved until you say Yes.
workflow.span.11: A verifiable task exists, not just a conversation.
workflow.pre.1: you › let's go with Postgres, not Mongo. we need transactions for orders. agent › That is an architectural decision, so an ADR first, not code. /projectstore:adr "Use Postgres for primary storage" → adr/use-postgres-for-primary-storage.md Context · Decision · Alternatives: MongoDB — rejected because … Save this file? Yes Edit before saving No
workflow.span.14: A person signs off on the scope and approach. Say No, and the vault stays exactly as it was.
workflow.h3.2: Check the decision while it is still cheap to change.
workflow.p.3: The critic is an agent that did not write the draft. It looks for weak assumptions, missing options and ways the plan could fail. It is told that a wrong approval costs 10–100× more than a wrong rejection.
workflow.span.16: Risks become part of the decision before implementation.
workflow.pre.2: 1. Alternatives. "MongoDB — no transactions" has been wrong since 4.0. The real reason is relational constraints. Say that, or the ADR misleads the next reader. 2. Consequences. What happens to the nightly reconcile job? Removed or kept? 3. Decision. "One transaction" for what? Order and lines, not payments. That boundary is the decision, and it is not written down.
workflow.span.21: The agent's verdict does not replace your approval. The author fixes the draft and never approves its own work.
workflow.h3.3: Approve. Put it in the backlog.
workflow.p.4: After the fixes, you see the file path and the full text, and say Yes. The same Yes updates the folder's index. The epic and the story go into the backlog. The board builds itself from the files; nobody keeps it up to date by hand.
workflow.span.23: Nothing is written without your Yes.
workflow.pre.3: agent › The ADR is fixed: boundary stated, nightly job retired. Save? Yes ✓ saved · ADR index updated /projectstore:epic PAY-001 "Order processing on Postgres" ✓ /projectstore:story PAY-001 "Transactional order writes" ✓ kanban.md · built from the story files ## Backlog - [ ] [[epics/PAY-001/stories/story-transactional-order-writes|PAY-001: Transactional order writes]] #p1
workflow.span.26: The board, indexes, link map and code map are built from the files. A hand edit cannot break them for good.
workflow.h3.4: Find out where exactly the code changes.
workflow.p.5: Before coding, the planner looks at where earlier epics landed in the code: which modules already own this area, and what to reuse. The plan goes into the story, and the story moves to in-progress.
workflow.span.28: The plan rests on how the project is built, not on a guess.
workflow.pre.4: earlier epics: BILL-001 → src/billing/ EXP-002 → adapters/csv/ Where. src/billing/orders/, next to BILL-001. No new module. Reuse. withTransaction() in src/db/tx.mjs already retries. Watch out. src/jobs/reconcile.mjs still runs nightly. The ADR retires it. Steps. migration → writer → rollback tests → remove the job. → saved to the story's plan · status: in-progress
workflow.span.31: The story links to its epic, its spec and the existing code. If a spec covers the story, the plan follows the spec.
workflow.h3.5: Check the code against the promised result.
workflow.p.6: The reviewer checks the real diff against every acceptance criterion, including those from the spec. "Done" needs proof: a test, a command that was run, or a specific piece of code.

workflow.span.38: Review happens before commit and before the story closes. The reviewer reports; it never edits or commits.
workflow.h3.6: Leave the next agent an entry point.
workflow.p.7: When the story closes, the board, the link map and the code map rebuild themselves. The next session starts from the list of decisions, not from nothing. Settled questions stay settled.

workflow.span.43: The clerk saves exactly what you approved. It makes no decisions of its own.
workflow.h4.1: Code without a story gets a reminder
workflow.p.8: Change three or more source files with no story in progress, and the agent gets one reminder: open a story first. Only edits that really happened count.
workflow.p.9: Every new ADR, spec, epic and research note stays marked "not reviewed" until the critic checks it. A short block in your agent's instructions sends it there before anyone treats it as final.
workflow.p.10: Does the board match the stories? Are links broken, or pointing at missing code? Is work going on with no story open? It runs when a session starts and speaks up only when something is wrong.
workflow.p.11: ↳ Decisions and writes go through approval. An independent agent helps to check; responsibility stays with the team.
artifacts.p.1: Read them in an editor, discuss them in a pull request, open them in Obsidian. The context is not tied to one tool.
artifacts.h3.1: Keep not only the choice but its reasons.
artifacts.p.2: An ADR records an architecture decision: the context, the options, the choice and its consequences. When a decision is reversed, its ADR is not deleted; it points to the one that replaced it. Six months later, nobody has the same argument again.

artifacts.p.3: A spec says how the system must behave, as numbered rules you can test. Several stories can implement one spec. Its checks are added to each story's, and a story cannot close while its spec is still a draft.

artifacts.div.2: A check that names no story applies to every story the spec covers.
artifacts.h3.3: Tie the task to a verifiable result.
artifacts.p.4: A story lives inside an epic. It holds the scope, the plan, the acceptance criteria and the proof. code_refs link it to real files. A story has two checkpoints: a plan before work starts, and a close with proof for each criterion.

artifacts.div.3: Evidence is added when the story closes: a test, a command or a line of code.
artifacts.h3.4: The board is built from the story files.
artifacts.p.5: Change the story's status or priority and watch the board move. The line below is exactly what lands in kanban.md. Edit the board by hand and you get a reminder to rebuild it. A stale board is something to fix, not a normal state.
artifacts.p.6: Stories marked superseded, deferred or parked leave the board instead of pretending to wait in line.
teams.p.1: The context belongs to the team, not to one developer's chat. ADRs and specs go through pull requests, like code. What gets reviewed is the reasoning.
teams.h3.1: Everyone sees more than their own part.
teams.p.2: The developer, the tech lead and QA work from the same decisions and criteria. A person without an agent needs only GitHub or a Markdown editor: it is just files.
teams.p.3: The context is available to the whole team, not only to the owner of the chat.
teams.span.8: An example of organizing the work, not live orchestration
teams.h3.2: Shared contracts. Separate areas of work.
teams.p.4: In one project, the API, Web and Platform teams run their own epics on top of shared ADRs and specs. A change to a shared contract is discussed in review with the teams that use it. ProjectStore shows which stories depend on it.
teams.p.5: Who owns which artifacts and who signs off on contracts is the team's call.
teams.span.12: shared ADRs and specs → review → merge
teams.span.13: Shared ADRs and specs · epics per team
teams.span.15: An example of organizing the work, not live orchestration
teams.p.6: The planner reads the decisions and the code map. The implementer reads the story and the spec. The reviewer reads the diff and the criteria. Each gets the context it needs, not the whole history of someone else's session. Sessions on the same vault warn each other.
teams.p.7: Launching agents and handing work between them is the job of your harness or orchestrator.
teams.span.19: read-only access via MCP or CLI

teams.title.1: Developers with their own agents bind to one vault in its own git repository. ADRs and specs are reviewed as pull requests. A teammate without an agent reviews on GitHub or in Obsidian.
teams.text.11: its own git repo · plain markdown
teams.figcaption.1: Put the vault in its own repository. Everyone installs ProjectStore, binds to the same vault and saves changes only after approval. A teammate without an agent reviews on GitHub or in Obsidian.
teams.h3.4: A team setup, step by step
teams.p.8: One repository of project documents per project, not per person. It sits next to the code repository.
teams.p.9: Each person runs /projectstore:bind in their own copy of the code. The setting stays on that machine and is not committed.
teams.h4.3: A branch and a pull request
teams.p.10: A person reviews each decision before it is accepted. The critic checks it before the pull request; your team reviews it inside.
teams.p.11: npx projectstore doctor --json runs in CI with no agent and no tokens. It fails the step when it finds problems. reconcile --write can rebuild the board there too.
teams.p.12: Two agents or two people in one vault at the same time is normal. Each session knows about the others, and a few simple rules keep them out of each other's way.
teams.li.1: No silent overwrites. Before saving a new file, ProjectStore checks that it does not exist yet. Two sessions on the same topic get a clash, not two copies.
teams.li.2: Each status line shows its own work. 2–6 sessions side by side each see exactly their own epic and story.
teams.li.3: Session names are offered, not imposed. Once a session settles on one piece of work, it suggests a name for it. Rarely: at most twice a session, 12 offers across nine recorded sessions.
teams.pre.1: developer A has worked on PAY-001 since 13:35. you open a second session: ⚠ Multi-session warning — 1 other projectstore session active. Run /projectstore:search <topic> before creating new artifacts. later, once your work settles on one epic: projectstore: this session looks like "pay-001-transactional-order-writes" → /rename pay-001-transactional-order-writes
teams.p.13: A real screenshot: this session's 📚 epic › story line, above the status bar you already use.
agents.h2.2: All but one may only read.
agents.p.1: The advisors check, plan and tidy up, and change nothing. One clerk saves only what you approved, after your Yes.
agents.td.1: After an ADR, spec, epic, story or design is written or changed
agents.td.2: Looks for weak spots, checks every claim against the source and asks how the plan could fail. No flattery.
agents.td.4: Before work on a story starts (story plan)
agents.td.5: Looks at where earlier epics live in the code. Says where the change belongs, what to reuse, what to watch out for and in what order to work.
agents.td.7: After code, before commit or story close
agents.td.8: Asks for proof on every acceptance criterion, including the spec's. Then checks correctness, regressions and tests.
agents.td.10: From time to time, before releases, after the vault grows fast
agents.td.11: Finds what no rule can catch: research notes that contradict an accepted ADR, duplicates, missing links, files ready to archive.
agents.td.13: Once, after binding an existing codebase
agents.td.14: Finds decisions nobody wrote down, in the code, config files and git history. Suggests ADRs for them, with evidence.
agents.td.16: Only inside a command flow, only after your Yes
agents.td.17: Saves exactly what you approved, nothing more. Then rebuilds the board and runs the checks. Writes nothing of its own and asks nothing.
agents.p.10: The default models are Claude Code's. In Codex each role is a skill of the same name, such as $projectstore-critic, that asks Codex to start the role; it uses the session's model unless you set one.
agents.p.2: Plans, critiques, writes code or checks the result. Each role is clear: advisors only read, the clerk only saves what was approved.
agents.p.3: Chosen for the task and the budget. /projectstore:agents configure sets one per agent. Changing it does not touch the project's history.
agents.p.4: Gives the agent its tools, permissions and session. The plugin installs into Claude Code and Codex. The CLI and MCP server are not tied to any one harness.
agents.p.5: * An illustration, not a ready integration. You set up each harness yourself. Any agent with a shell or MCP can read the same facts through the read-only MCP tools below.
agents.p.6: Every command and agent, automatic reminders, the status line and vault setup. The ready-made way into the loop.
agents.p.11: The commands and roles as skills, such as $projectstore-doctor and $projectstore-critic, with lifecycle hooks and the agents block. docs/harnesses.md says what has been verified so far.
agents.p.7: The CLI reads the vault and makes only the writes you ask for, with JSON output. The MCP server gives any agent the read-only tools.
agents.p.8: Gemini CLI, OpenCode and the rest: the Markdown files work anywhere, and the CLI and MCP read the same vault. Native adapters for them do not ship yet.
agents.p.9: ↳ ProjectStore is shared project context and a way of working. It is not an agent orchestrator. The vault goes with you: switch models tomorrow and the project continues.
cost.p.1: Running the loop is not free, and this page will not pretend otherwise.
cost.p.2: Measured on the ProjectStore repo itself. Here the tool builds itself, and every change goes through the full loop, critic included.
cost.p.3: What you get: a project manager and a systems analyst who never forget to write things down, run by the agent you already pay for. The files are your real backlog, review record and decision log, not private notes.
start.p.1: Install it in Claude Code or Codex, pick a folder for the vault and ask the agent to write the first ADR. No need to move the whole project history in one evening. The archaeologist agent can help with that later.
start.p.2: Install the projectstore plugin from https://github.com/SmartAndPoint/ProjectStore and set it up for this project.
start.span.8: Type the commands in Claude Code
start.p.3: The vault path is an example. Bind then asks a few setup questions and shows what each step will write. Turn on auto-update: /plugin → Marketplaces → SmartAndPoint.
start.p.4: Run it from your project folder. It adds the plugin to Claude Code for this checkout only and prints every command before running it. Then restart Claude Code and bind a vault.
start.span.16: Terminal · Node.js 20+ · in your project folder
start.p.5: Then restart Codex, approve the ProjectStore hooks when it asks, and run $projectstore-bind ~/Documents/my-project-vault. docs/harnesses.md says what has been verified so far.

start.span.14: Every write is shown before it is saved. Nothing is written without your Yes.
questions.p.2: No. A memory plugin remembers what the agent said. ProjectStore records what the project decided, as reviewed documents with a status and a date. New work then goes through those documents. The difference shows when you switch models: memory belongs to a model, a vault belongs to the project.
questions.summary.2: Does it replace Jira, Linear or a task tracker?
questions.p.3: Not necessarily. ProjectStore links decisions, specs, stories and code. You can keep your tracker for planning, and keep the technical context in the vault. There is no automatic sync with other trackers, but a story can hold a link to its ticket.
questions.p.4: No. The vault is an ordinary folder of Markdown files. Open it in an editor, browse it on GitHub, or use Obsidian if you like its graph and board. Without the plugin, the files stay just as readable.
questions.summary.4: Does it ever write without asking?
questions.p.5: No. Every new file or edit is shown to you first, with its path and full text. Then it waits for Yes, Edit before saving, or No. The helpers that watch the conversation only suggest a command. The only agent that can write, the clerk, runs after your Yes and saves exactly what you approved.
questions.summary.5: What happens if two agents change the same file?
questions.p.6: Work in separate branches, then review and resolve git conflicts as usual. In one local vault, sessions warn each other and new files are never silently overwritten. But this is not a lock, and it does not sync between machines.
questions.summary.6: What if someone hand-edits a vault file?
questions.p.7: That is allowed, because banning it never works. You get a reminder to run reconcile. doctor spots a board or index that no longer matches the files, and reconcile rebuilds them from the source files.
questions.summary.7: Where does the project context go?
questions.p.8: ProjectStore needs no server: the vault lives where you put it. Which files the agent reads and what reaches the model provider depends on your harness and its permissions. Keep secrets out of project documents and check your team's access rules.
questions.p.9: No. Critic and reviewer runs use your model's budget: 22.5% of spend on the ProjectStore repo itself, typically 10–15% of a weekly limit. The routine checks, doctor and reconcile, use no AI. Match the depth of the process to the risk of the change.
questions.summary.9: What if we move from Claude Code to another agent?
questions.p.10: Nothing is lost: the vault is plain Markdown in git. The automatic part, the commands, the roles and the reminders, installs into Claude Code and Codex, and the two can work one project side by side. Any other agent reads the same facts through the CLI or the MCP server.

meta.description: ProjectStore is a project workflow plugin for Claude Code and Codex. It keeps your project's decisions, specs and stories as Markdown in git, and your agent follows the process engineering teams have used for decades: decide, review, build, verify. Now it takes minutes.

why.aria-label.1: Three lanes: humans with a process are slow but keep context; agents without a process are fast but every session re-decides; agents with ProjectStore are fast and keep context.
